     6	## History of Vaccine Development
     7	
     8	The first vaccine was created by Edward Jenner in 1796 against smallpox, using cowpox to trigger immunity. It took nearly a century before the next vaccine (rabies) was developed, because scientists didn't yet understand germ theory. Once Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch established germ theory in the late 19th century, vaccines for rabies, cholera, and anthrax followed.
     9	
    10	The timeline from pathogen identification to vaccine licensure has shortened dramatically over the past 140 years:
    11	
    12	| Disease | Pathogen Identified | Vaccine Licensed | Gap (Years) |
    13	|---|---|---|---|
    14	| Typhoid fever | 1884 | 1989 | 105 |
    15	| Meningitis | 1889 | 1981 | 92 |
    16	| Whooping cough | 1906 | 1948 | 42 |
    17	| Polio | 1908 | 1955 | 47 |
    18	| Measles | 1953 | 1963 | 10 |
    19	| Chickenpox | 1953 | 1995 | 42 |
    20	| Hepatitis B | 1965 | 1981 | 16 |
    21	| Ebola | 1976 | 2019 | 43 |
    22	| COVID-19 | 2020 | 2020 | <1 |
    23	
    24	![Vaccination innovation timeline from 1880 to 2020](./assets/figure_3.jpg)
    25	
    26	Modern tools — advanced microscopy, genome sequencing, mRNA technology, and virus-like particles — have enabled faster and more precise vaccine design.
    27	
    28	## Dramatic Disease Reductions in the United States
    29	
    30	Data from Roush and Murphy (2007) shows the reduction in cases and deaths for vaccine-preventable diseases in the US after vaccine introduction. Several diseases achieved 100% elimination of both cases and deaths.
    31	
    32	| Disease | Pre-Vaccine Cases (per million/yr) | Post-Vaccine Cases (per million/yr) | Case Reduction | Pre-Vaccine Deaths (per million/yr) | Death Reduction |
    33	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
    34	| Diphtheria | 158 | 0 | 100% | 13.7 | 100% |
    35	| Measles | 3,044 | 0.2 | 99.99% | 2.5 | 100% |
    36	| Smallpox | 250 | 0 | 100% | 2.9 | 100% |
    37	| Acute polio | 141 | 0 | 100% | 10 | 100% |
    38	| Pertussis | 1,534 | 52 | 96.6% | 30.8 | 99.7% |
    39	| Rubella | 242 | 0.04 | 99.98% | 0.09 | 100% |
    40	| Hepatitis A | 465 | 51 | 89% | 0.5 | 88.7% |
    41	| Acute hepatitis B | 273 | 44 | 83.9% | 1 | 83.6% |
    42	| Pneumococcal | 233 | 139 | 40.5% | 24 | 31.3% |
    43	
    44	![US vaccine-preventable disease reductions](./assets/figure_1.jpg)
    45	
    46	## Measles Elimination Across US States
    47	
    48	A heatmap of measles cases per 100,000 across all 50 US states from 1929 to 2022 shows the dramatic impact of vaccination. Three key milestones transformed the landscape:
    49	
    50	- **1963**: First measles vaccine developed by John Enders
    51	- **1971**: MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) vaccine developed by Maurice Hilleman
    52	- **1980**: Vaccination became mandatory for children entering kindergarten
    53	
    54	Before 1963, nearly every state experienced high measles incidence (100–1,000+ cases per 100,000). After the 1980 mandate, cases dropped to near zero across all states, with only sporadic outbreaks.
    55	
    56	![Measles heatmap across US states](./assets/figure_2.jpg)
    57	
    58	## Smallpox Eradication: The Greatest Vaccination Success
    59	
    60	Smallpox was declared eradicated worldwide in 1980 — the only human disease to be fully eliminated through vaccination. Key factors enabling eradication: the virus infected only humans, symptoms were distinguishable, and the vaccine was cheap and effective. The WHO passed a resolution to eradicate smallpox in 1959, launched an intensified campaign in 1967, and the last natural case occurred in Somalia in 1977.
    61	
    62	## Herd Immunity and Remaining Challenges
    63	
    64	Vaccines protect not only individuals but entire communities through herd immunity. When enough people are vaccinated, pathogens cannot spread effectively, shielding those who cannot be vaccinated — newborns, immunocompromised individuals, and cancer patients on chemotherapy.
    65	
    66	However, significant challenges remain. Pneumococcal disease has seen only a 40.5% reduction in cases and 31.3% in deaths. Hepatitis A and B still show incomplete control. Globally, not everyone has access to vaccines, supply shortages put children at risk, and poor scientific understanding can reduce trust and uptake.
    67	
    68	## Key Findings
    69	
    70	- **Vaccines achieved 100% elimination** of cases and deaths for diphtheria, smallpox, and both forms of polio in the US.
    71	- **Vaccine development timelines have collapsed** from over 100 years (typhoid) to under 1 year (COVID-19), driven by mRNA technology and genomic tools.
    72	- **Measles cases dropped to near zero** across all 50 US states following the 1980 kindergarten vaccination mandate.
    73	- **Smallpox remains the only human disease eradicated** through vaccination, certified in 1980 after a global campaign.
    74	- **Gaps persist** for pneumococcal disease (40.5% case reduction), hepatitis A (89%), and hepatitis B (83.9%), highlighting the need for improved access, coverage, and newer vaccines.

- **Layout**: Top-bottom split — horizontal bar chart top (y=80–420), annotations bottom (y=440–640)

- **Layout**: Full-width structured data table

- **Content**:

  - Source: Roush and Murphy (2007)
- **Template**: `03_content.svg`

#### Slide 04 — Measles Heatmap States (measles-heatmap-states)

- **Layout**: Left-right split — heatmap visualization left (60%), milestone annotations right (40%)
- **Title**: "Measles Cases Collapsed Across All 50 US States After Vaccine Mandates"
- **Content**:

  - Vertical milestone lines/labels at 1963, 1971, 1980
  - Right panel: Three milestone callouts with year + event
    - 1963: First measles vaccine (John Enders)
    - 1971: MMR vaccine (Maurice Hilleman)
    - 1980: Mandatory kindergarten vaccination
  - Bottom note: "Before 1963, nearly every state experienced high measles incidence. After the 1980 mandate, cases dropped to near zero across all states."
- **Template**: `03_content.svg`

#### Slide 05 — Smallpox Eradication Story (smallpox-eradication-story)

- **Layout**: Top-bottom split — timeline top, key factors bottom
- **Title**: "Smallpox: The Only Human Disease Eradicated Through Vaccination"
- **Content**:
  - Timeline: 1959 → 1967 → 1977 → 1980 with event labels
    - 1959: WHO resolution to eradicate smallpox
    - 1967: Intensified global campaign launched
    - 1977: Last natural case (Somalia)
    - 1980: Certified eradicated worldwide
  - Bottom: Three key factors in cards
    - Virus infected only humans
    - Symptoms were distinguishable
    - Vaccine was cheap and effective
  - Source note: "Smallpox remains the only human disease fully eliminated through vaccination."
- **Template**: `03_content.svg`

#### Slide 06 — Herd Immunity Mechanism (herd-immunity-mechanism)

- **Layout**: Left-right split (5:5) — diagram left, explanation right
- **Title**: "Herd Immunity: How Vaccinating Many Protects the Most Vulnerable"
- **Content**:
  - Left: Simple population diagram — grid of ~25 person icons
    - ~80% filled teal (vaccinated/protected)
    - ~20% outlined gray (vulnerable: newborns, immunocompromised, chemotherapy patients)
    - Shield icon overlay on teal group
    - Pathogen "blocked" visualization (red X at boundary)
  - Right: Text explanation
    - "When enough people are vaccinated, pathogens cannot spread effectively."
    - Bullet list of shielded groups:
      - Newborns too young for vaccines
      - Immunocompromised individuals
      - Cancer patients on chemotherapy
  - Template: `03_content.svg`

#### Slide 07 — Remaining Challenges (remaining-challenges)

- **Layout**: Matrix grid — 3 KPI cards top, narrative text bottom
- **Title**: "Gaps Persist: Pneumococcal Disease Shows Only 40% Case Reduction"
- **Content**:
  - Three data cards:
    - Pneumococcal: 40.5% case reduction | 31.3% death reduction (red warning)
    - Hepatitis A: 89% case reduction | 88.7% death reduction (amber)
    - Acute Hepatitis B: 83.9% case reduction | 83.6% death reduction (amber)
  - Bottom narrative:
    - "Globally, not everyone has access to vaccines."
    - "Supply shortages put children at risk."
    - "Poor scientific understanding can reduce trust and uptake."
- **Template**: `03_content.svg`

#### Slide 08 — Takeaways and Priorities (takeaways-and-priorities)

- **Layout**: Single column centered — 5 takeaway cards stacked
- **Title**: "Key Takeaways: Vaccines Have Eliminated Deadly Diseases — But the Job Isn't Done"
- **Content**:
  - 5 numbered takeaways:
    1. **100% elimination** achieved for diphtheria, smallpox, and both forms of polio in the US.
    2. **Development timelines collapsed** from over 100 years (typhoid) to under 1 year (COVID-19), driven by mRNA technology and genomic tools.
    3. **Measles cases dropped to near zero** across all 50 US states following the 1980 kindergarten vaccination mandate.
    4. **Smallpox remains the only human disease eradicated** through vaccination, certified in 1980 after a global campaign.
    5. **Gaps persist** for pneumococcal disease (40.5%), hepatitis A (89%), and hepatitis B (83.9%), highlighting the need for improved access, coverage, and newer vaccines.
  - Closing call to action: "Global health systems must prioritize equitable access, supply chain resilience, and public trust to finish the job."

    56	- **Comparison baselines**: Mark industry average / target values with gray dashed lines
    57	- **Consistent units**: Maintain the same numeric units and precision within a chart
    58	
    59	### 4. Table Design
    60	
    61	Consulting reports frequently use tables for precise data:
    62	
    63	| Design Element | Specification |
    64	|----------------|---------------|
    65	| Header | Dark background + white text, font-weight="bold" |
    66	| Zebra striping | Alternate rows with `fill-opacity="0.05"` light background |
    67	| Number alignment | Numbers right-aligned, text left-aligned |
    68	| Highlighted row | Mark key rows with accent color `fill-opacity="0.1"` |
    69	| Borders | Use horizontal lines only to separate rows; avoid full grid lines |

    73	## Consulting-specific Layout Patterns
    74	
    75	### MECE Decomposition Tree
    76	
    77	Main trunk on the left, branches expanding rightward — mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive:
    78	
    79	```
    80	Main metric ──┬── Branch A (45%)
    81	              ├── Branch B (30%)
    82	              ├── Branch C (20%)
    83	              └── Branch D (5%)
    84	```
    85	
    86	- Use `<line>` to connect trunk to branches
    87	- Each branch has a `<rect>` container + percentage annotation
    88	- Sum must = 100% (or explicitly label "Other")
    89	
    90	### Driver Factor Tree
    91	
    92	Top-level metric → decomposed factors → actions. Ideal for performance attribution analysis:
    93	
    94	```
    95	Revenue growth 15%
    96	  ├── Average order value +8%  → Premium product line expansion
    97	  ├── Customer count +5%       → New channel acquisition
    98	  └── Repurchase rate +2%      → Loyalty program optimization
    99	```
   100	
   101	### Left-chart Right-text (Chart Interpretation)
   102	
   103	Core consulting report layout: chart on the left, key insights on the right:
   104	
   105	```
   106	Chart area: x=40, y=120, w=700, h=480
   107	Insight area: x=780, y=120, w=460, h=480
   108	  - Core conclusion (bold, 16px)
   109	  - 3-5 bullet points (14px)
   110	  - Data source (12px, gray)
   111	```

   115	## Professional Expression Standards
   116	
   117	### Page Titles
   118	
   119	Consulting-style page titles should be **assertion headlines**, not descriptive titles:
   120	
   121	| Type | Descriptive (avoid) | Assertion (recommended) |
   122	|------|---------------------|------------------------|
   123	| Market | "Market Overview" | "Domestic market grows 23% YoY, significantly outpacing global average" |
   124	| Competition | "Competitive Analysis" | "Three major competitors show clear weaknesses in channel coverage" |
   125	| Finance | "Financial Data" | "Gross margin improved for four consecutive quarters, breaking industry ceiling" |
   126	
   127	### Data Source Attribution
   128	
   129	Every data-containing page must include a source note at the bottom:
   130	
   131	```xml
   132	<text x="40" y="700" font-size="10" fill="#94A3B8">
   133	  Source: National Bureau of Statistics 2025 Annual Report; Internal team analysis
   134	</text>
   135	```
   136	
   137	### Key Takeaway Box
   138	
   139	Consulting-style content pages should include a **Takeaway Box** below the title:
   140	
   141	```
   142	Position: x=40, y=80, w=1200, h=50
   143	Background: Light theme color (fill-opacity="0.08")
   144	Text: 14-16px, one-sentence summary of the page's core takeaway
   145	```
   146

   148	
   149	## Speaker Notes Style
   150	
   151	### Narrative Tone
   152	
   153	Consultant-style speaker notes use a **conclusion-driven** approach — state the conclusion first, then present supporting evidence. Professional, concise, and persuasive tone.
   154	
   155	### Stage Direction Markers
   156	
   157	| Marker | Purpose | Example |
   158	|--------|---------|---------|
   159	| `[Pause]` | Silence after key conclusions, let the audience absorb | "This means our market share is being eroded. [Pause]" |
   160	| `[Data]` | Cue to verbalize numbers conversationally | "[Data] 85% → more than eight out of ten customers reported this issue" |
   161	| `[Transition]` | Bridge from previous page, must be at start of each page's text | "[Transition] Based on that analysis, let's look at specific recommendations." |
   162	
   163	### Notes Writing Guidelines
   164	
   165	- **Conclusion first**: The first sentence of each page's notes is the core takeaway
   166	- **Conversational data**: 30% → "roughly one-third", 85% → "more than eight out of ten", 2.5x → "two and a half times"
   167	- **Evidence follows immediately**: After the conclusion, provide 2-3 supporting data points/facts
   168	- **Professional terminology**: Use terms like "insight", "driver", "key lever" etc.
   169	- **Key points structure**: `Key points: (1) Core conclusion (2) Supporting data (3) Next steps`
   170	
   171	### Notes Example
   172	
   173	```markdown
   174	# 03_key_findings
   175	
   176	[Transition] Based on our market scan, we have distilled three key findings.
   177	
   178	First, the primary growth driver is shifting from acquisition to retention.
   179	[Data] New customer acquisition cost rose nearly 40% year-over-year, yet improved repurchase rates contributed over 60% of revenue growth. [Pause]
   180	
   181	Second, lower-tier market growth significantly outpaces tier-1 and tier-2 cities.
   182	Third, the 25-35 female user segment has an ARPU 1.8x the overall average.
   183	
   184	Key points: (1) Growth engine shifting from acquisition to retention (2) Lower-tier market opportunity window (3) High-value user persona
   185	Duration: 2 minutes
   186	```

     7	## 1. SVG Banned Features Blacklist
     8	
     9	The following features are **absolutely forbidden** when generating SVGs — PPT export will break if any are used:

    12	|----------------|-------------|

    14	| `mask` | Masks |
    15	| `<style>` | Embedded stylesheets |
    16	| `class` | CSS selector attributes (`id` inside `<defs>` is a legitimate reference and is NOT banned) |
    17	| External CSS | External stylesheet links |
    18	| `<foreignObject>` | Embedded external content |
    19	| `<symbol>` + `<use>` | Symbol reference reuse |
    20	| `textPath` | Text along a path |
    21	| `@font-face` | Custom font declarations |
    22	| `<animate*>` / `<set>` | SVG animations |
    23	| `<script>` / event attributes | Scripts and interactivity |
    24	| `marker` / `marker-end` | Line endpoint markers |
    25	| `<iframe>` | Embedded frames |

   108	## 6. Shadow & Overlay Techniques
   109	
   110	> `<mask>` elements and `<image opacity="...">` are banned. Always use stacked `<rect>` or gradient overlays instead (see §2).
   111	
   112	### Shadow
   113	
   114	#### Filter Soft Shadow — Recommended
   115	
   116	Best for: cards, floating panels, elevated elements. `svg_to_shapes.py` automatically converts `feGaussianBlur` + `feOffset` into native PPTX `<a:outerShdw>`.
   117	
   118	```xml
   119	<defs>
   120	  <filter id="softShadow" x="-15%" y="-15%" width="140%" height="140%">
   121	    <feGaussianBlur in="SourceAlpha" stdDeviation="8"/>
   122	    <feOffset dx="0" dy="4" result="offsetBlur"/>
   123	    <feFlood flood-color="#000000" flood-opacity="0.08" result="shadowColor"/>
   124	    <feComposite in="shadowColor" in2="offsetBlur" operator="in" result="shadow"/>
   125	    <feMerge>
   126	      <feMergeNode in="shadow"/>
   127	      <feMergeNode in="SourceGraphic"/>
   128	    </feMerge>
   129	  </filter>
   130	</defs>
   131	<rect x="60" y="60" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#FFFFFF" filter="url(#softShadow)"/>
   132	```
   133	
   134	Recommended parameters:
   135	```
   136	stdDeviation:   6–10     (smaller = crisper, larger = softer)
   137	flood-opacity:  0.06–0.12  (keep low for a premium feel)
   138	dy:             3–6      (vertical > horizontal for natural top-light)
   139	dx:             0–2
   140	```
   141	
   142	#### Colored Shadow
   143	
   144	Best for: accent buttons, brand-colored cards. Use the element's own color family instead of black.

   146	```xml

   149	  <feOffset dx="0" dy="6" result="offsetBlur"/>
   150	  <feFlood flood-color="#1A73E8" flood-opacity="0.20" result="shadowColor"/>
   151	  <feComposite in="shadowColor" in2="offsetBlur" operator="in" result="shadow"/>
   152	  <feMerge>
   153	    <feMergeNode in="shadow"/>
   154	    <feMergeNode in="SourceGraphic"/>
   155	  </feMerge>
   156	</filter>
   157	```
   158	
   159	Replace `flood-color` with the element's brand color; keep `flood-opacity` between 0.12–0.20.
   160	
   161	#### Layered Rect Shadow — High-Compatibility Fallback
   162	
   163	Best for: maximum compatibility with older PowerPoint versions. Stack 2–3 semi-transparent rectangles behind the main card:
   164

   168	<rect x="65" y="69" width="400" height="240" rx="14" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="0.05"/>
   169	<rect x="62" y="66" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#1A73E8" fill-opacity="0.04"/>
   170	<!-- Main card -->
   171	<rect x="60" y="60" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#FFFFFF"/>
   172	```

   176	#### Linear Gradient Overlay — Most Common
   177

   185	    <stop offset="55%"  stop-color="#1A1A2E" stop-opacity="0.30"/>
   186	    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#1A1A2E" stop-opacity="0"/>
   187	  </linearGradient>
   188	</defs>
   189	<rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" fill="url(#imgOverlay)"/>
   190	```

   206	#### Radial Gradient Overlay — Vignette Effect

   208	Best for: full-screen atmosphere slides; draws attention to the center.

# 01_title_slide

Welcome to this data-driven briefing on the power of vaccination. Over the next twenty minutes, we will trace the trajectory of vaccine development from Edward Jenner's first smallpox vaccine in 1796 to the record-breaking COVID-19 vaccines developed in under a year. Our goal is to quantify the dramatic reductions in disease burden that vaccines have achieved, examine the mechanisms that make elimination possible, and confront the remaining challenges in global coverage.

Key points: (1) Scope spans 1796–2020 (2) Focus on data-backed disease elimination evidence (3) Remaining gaps require policy attention
Duration: 1.5 minutes

---

# 02_vaccine_timeline

[Transition] To understand how far we've come, let's look at the accelerating pace of vaccine development itself.

The timeline from pathogen identification to vaccine licensure has collapsed by more than a hundredfold. [Data] Typhoid fever took 105 years; meningitis took 92. Even polio required 47 years. But COVID-19 went from pathogen identification to licensed vaccine in under one year. [Pause] This acceleration was driven by mRNA technology, genome sequencing, and virus-like particle platforms that simply did not exist for earlier vaccines.

Key points: (1) Pre-germ-theory era: 40–100+ year gaps (2) Modern era: 10–43 years (3) COVID-19: <1 year represents a paradigm shift
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 03_us_disease_elimination

[Transition] Faster development is meaningless without real-world impact. Let's examine what happened after vaccines reached the US population.

The data from Roush and Murphy is striking: four diseases achieved 100% elimination of both cases and deaths. [Data] Diphtheria fell from 158 cases per million to zero. Smallpox and acute polio both reached zero. Rubella deaths dropped 100%. [Pause] Yet not all vaccines perform equally. Pneumococcal disease shows only a 40.5% case reduction and 31.3% death reduction — a clear signal that some pathogens require newer or better vaccines, and that coverage matters enormously.

Key points: (1) 100% elimination for diphtheria, smallpox, polio, rubella (2) Measles at 99.99% cases, 100% deaths (3) Pneumococcal remains a major gap
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 04_measles_heatmap

[Transition] National averages can hide state-level variation. The measles story shows what happens when policy follows science.

Before 1963, nearly every US state experienced high measles incidence — 100 to over 1,000 cases per 100,000 people. [Data] The 1963 Enders vaccine, the 1971 Hilleman MMR, and the 1980 kindergarten mandate created a three-step collapse. [Pause] By the 1980s, the heatmap went from deep red across all 50 states to near-white — near elimination — with only sporadic outbreaks. This is one of the most dramatic public health transformations in US history.

Key points: (1) Three milestones: 1963, 1971, 1980 (2) State-level mandate drove near-zero incidence (3) Policy + science = elimination
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 05_smallpox_eradication

[Transition] Measles was eliminated in the US, but smallpox was eliminated everywhere. Let's examine why.

Smallpox remains the only human disease fully eradicated through vaccination. [Data] The WHO passed a resolution in 1959, intensified the campaign in 1967, and the last natural case occurred in Somalia in 1977. Certification came in 1980. [Pause] Three factors made this possible: the virus infected only humans, symptoms were clearly visible, and the vaccine was cheap and highly effective. These conditions are rare — which is why smallpox stands alone.

Key points: (1) Timeline: 1959 → 1967 → 1977 → 1980 (2) Three unique enabling factors (3) No other human disease has been fully eradicated since
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 06_herd_immunity

[Transition] Elimination is not just about protecting the vaccinated individual. It's about protecting those who cannot be vaccinated.

Herd immunity is the population-level shield created when enough people are immune that pathogens cannot sustain transmission. [Data] When roughly 80% or more of a community is vaccinated, the remaining 20% — newborns, immunocompromised patients, and cancer patients on chemotherapy — are protected not by their own immunity, but by the community's. [Pause] This is the ethical and epidemiological foundation of universal vaccination policy.

Key points: (1) Herd immunity protects the most vulnerable (2) Three shielded groups: newborns, immunocompromised, chemotherapy patients (3) High coverage is a community responsibility
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 07_remaining_challenges

[Transition] Despite these successes, the data makes clear that the job is not finished.

Pneumococcal disease shows only a 40.5% case reduction — the largest remaining gap in our dataset. Hepatitis A and B both sit in the 83–89% range, still leaving millions at risk. [Data] Globally, access inequality means not everyone receives vaccines. Supply shortages put children at risk in low-resource settings. And poor scientific understanding can erode trust and reduce uptake. [Pause] These are not scientific problems alone — they are policy, logistics, and communication challenges.

Key points: (1) Pneumococcal: 40.5% case / 31.3% death reduction (2) Hepatitis A/B: ~84–89% reductions (3) Three barriers: access, supply, trust
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 08_takeaways

[Transition] Let's bring this together into five clear takeaways and a forward-looking call to action.

First, vaccines have achieved 100% elimination of multiple deadly diseases in the US. Second, development timelines collapsed from over 100 years to under 1 year. Third, state-level mandates drove measles to near zero across all 50 states. Fourth, smallpox remains our only globally eradicated human disease — a proof of concept. Fifth, gaps persist for pneumococcal disease and hepatitis. [Pause] The call to action is clear: global health systems must prioritize equitable access, supply chain resilience, and public trust. The science has done its part. Now policy and implementation must finish the job.

Key points: (1) Five evidence-based takeaways (2) Science succeeded; implementation must follow (3) Call to action: access, resilience, trust
Duration: 2 minutes
